correctness.rationale: The displayed edge potential sums to zero, with part sums 1/N and -1/N at the two endpoint parts and zero elsewhere. The multipartite Laplacian therefore sends it to the unit source-sink divergence. Signed edge gradients give the cut column; summing the disjoint cross-endpoint-part and endpoint-to-other-part types, using (N-1)/(N-a) >= 1/(N-b) and its reverse, gives F_N(a)+F_N(b). The cut diagonal is (N-1)/N times [1/(N-a)+1/(N-b)], and the complementary norm changes the column sum by 1-2Q_ee. Both matrices are symmetric. For x=N-a and y=N-b in actual distinct parts, x,y>=2 and x+y>=N+1, so xy-2(N-1)=(x-2)(y-2)+2(x+y-N-1)>=0; this gives the two-largest cut rule. In K_(k,2,1), H_N(2)-H_N(1)=(N-6)/(N(N-2)) and H_N(1)-H_N(k)=F_N(k)-F_N(1)=(k-1)/(3N). Thus the cycle maximizing pair is unique even at k=3, when the two selected component scores tie; the strict cut ranking and the two rational norms also check. Independent rational grounded systems reproduced both column sums and cut diagonals on all 780 columns in 45 graphs, with direct maximizing-edge tests including k=3,4,5,6,8,13, via python3 /workspace/branches/reproduce_45.py 4.
residual_risks: The independent computations corroborate the proof; they are not the all-size argument. The conclusion is for the canonical Euclidean projections, not optimization over other projections.
